Lovecraft, as with any source material, has generated adaptations of varying quality. However, the spirit of Cosmicism clearly lives on in countless ways. Both In the Mouth of Madness and The Thing prove to be exemplary pieces of Cosmicism. Aliens reawakening, crushing existential horrors, and endless madness dominate these two journeys into the truly unthinkable.

John Carpenter's The Thing is an adaptation of John W. Campbell, Junior's Who Goes There?, in turn likely inspired by Lovecraft. My favorite film, it truly opened the cosmic for discussion, though initially attacked by critics and audiences. The ultimate unknown is an alien presence, truly indistinguishable from a human being. Hundreds of thousands of years before our modern sciences, an alien race had mastered interstellar time-travel- what might the galaxy be now?

If we are so truly imitateable, then what significance do we hold? The creature can so easily become us, and yet, we cannot become it. We are doomed to inhabit static bodies, with a central brain and ordinary nerves. The Thing, perhaps, carries its mind in every part of itself. There is too much we do not know about this magnificent being to ever guess at its true nature.

Similarly to another Lovecraftian masterwork, In the Mouth of Madness, The Thing captures a sense of ordinary reality torn away from us. The alien creature truly touches upon the uncanny valley; it unceasingly creates a nightmarish paradox of our own identity. What is humanity? What is life itself? These things are mysteries eternal, for we cannot know the Thing's processes.

Indeed, Lovecraft's influence can be seen in the helpless reactions of the characters. Madness ensues; two-thirds of the way through the film, a lynch mobbed is formed. The ensuing chaos among characters later revealed to be human show's the Thing's masterful chess play. The creature often, in human form, turns down opportunities for leadership, remains quiet during fights, and allows paranoia to reach deadly levels without interference. The men's fear overwhelms them; the mounting horror drives away rational thought in the face of the eldritch. We are now faced by our own paranoia about ourselves and those around us...

Much of the film echoes At the Mountains of Madness, as does the original work. A group of scientists and workers uncover an unthinkable alien menace... And do not realize that it still lives. Ancient history, questions of identity, and futile struggles to cling to humanity ensue in all three works.

While these works do not overtly speak of Lovecraft, any keen viewer will likely be imbued with a sense of the malignant Outside. My own first viewings were enough to chill me with cosmic delight, though I was well-versed in cosmic horror at that point. Cosmic horror, with its implied conspiracies in every nook and corner, inhuman whispers of an inhuman future, and blackest implications of our own place in the cosmos, generates nothing if not some small intrigue. The shared nature of the Mythos, with its components that have now become prevalent in popular culture, perhaps creates a thrill of recognition in the uninitiated. Few genres have so shaped fantasy, science fiction, and horror cultures. The fear of the unknown has had the strongest pull upon humanity imaginable. We are forever frightened of the impenetrable darkness, for how shall we know what lies beyond? Robbed of our senses, we are left bereaved of our stability in the world. The Thing may well be hiding within any of those black corners, in the closet, under the bed... We cannot know whether those things lurking might become us, or us them. The unknown is infinitely repulsive to our feeble minds, and modern works of horror exemplify this yet.

As Lovecraft's fungoid influence grows, spreading from deep, drenched caverns to the surface as though by underground mycelium, so too does our awareness of the existential horrors we cannot bear to face. No longer do films about little green men of human intelligence dominate; as with The Thing and The Bodysnatchers, we are faced with species that may simply be to us as we are to worms. The Thing does not wish to hold dialogue with us, nor is it purposefully, humanly sadistic; it merely operates according to its own dictates of evolution.

Lovecraft, Robert E. Howard, and Clark Ashton Smith examined a truth no one wants to submit to, but which fascinates us endlessly: There is no loving God. There is no objective morality, no karma, and no eternal reward. We, like the Thing, and as with John Trent of Mouth of Madness, are so much miniscule meat in a senseless multiverse. Our suppositions of importance are nothing more than delusion, and we seek this obscene, forbidden revelation in fiction. To stand on that verge of madness and despair is thrilling; to taste of the unbound Outside is so vulgar and taboo as to be a terrible pleasure.

Readers have begun to discover the secret thrill of participating in a hiddrn cosmos of conspiracy; it is delicious to contemplate who among us might be an alien or a deity. The shared nature of the Mythos gives rise to a certainty that there is indeed some validity to our paranoid claims; the universe indeed plots against our happiness and fortune. Perhaps it even gives the reader or watcher a sense of order: We may not be the denizens of a living, loving God, but we nonetheless find ourselves guided by some higher order. This, of course, is completely false: The Old Ones have no ordered motivation, and no logic save that of entropy.

Of every dark genre, only Cosmicism and the works of Lovecraft are ungraspable to even their strictest disciples. We may comprehend that these alien beings exist, but we shall never grasp their Truth. The reader cannot comprehend the mind of the Thing, nor can the watcher truly understand what Sutter Cane has become in Mouth of Madness. We, the blind idiot species, are left to cower in the planet's warm places, asking why without ever receiving an answer from the stars.

This is the real reason astronauts float inside the International Space Station (ISS) - they, and the vehicle are in free-fall. It isn't because there is "zero gravity" in space, as is often said. In fact, while the acceleration of gravity on the Earth surface is about 9.81 m/s^2, at the altitude of the ISS the acceleration of gravity has only dropped to about 8.75 m/s^2. Over time, the thin mist of gas molecules in orbit decelerate the spacecraft via drag forces. That deceleration causes the vehicle to lower its orbit. Eventually the vehicle needs to fire thrusters to re-accelerate to the appropriate velocity.
